client_need: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
stem: A nurse is preparing to change the dressing over a central venous catheter insertion site. Which technique best reflects current CDC recommendations?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, maintain aseptic technique, cleanse the site with an appropriate antiseptic, and apply a sterile catheter-site dressing; either clean or sterile gloves may be used for the dressing change.
options.B: Use clean technique without attention to asepsis because the central catheter was inserted under sterile conditions.
options.C: Wear sterile gloves, but omit skin antisepsis if the insertion site has no redness or drainage.
options.D: Use maximal sterile barrier precautions with cap, sterile gown, full-body drape, and sterile gloves for every routine dressing change.

rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends hand hygiene before and after dressing an intravascular catheter, maintenance of aseptic technique during catheter care, skin antisepsis during dressing changes, and use of a sterile gauze or sterile transparent semipermeable dressing. For routine intravascular-catheter dressing changes, CDC states that either clean or sterile gloves may be worn. B is incorrect because aseptic technique remains necessary during catheter care. C is incorrect because skin antisepsis is part of dressing-change care even when the site appears normal. D confuses routine dressing changes with central-line insertion, for which maximal sterile barrier precautions are recommended.
educational_objective: For central-line dressing changes, maintain aseptic technique with hand hygiene, appropriate skin antisepsis, and a sterile dressing; do not assume sterile gloves or maximal sterile barrier precautions are universally required for every routine dressing change.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source_document_title: Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections — Summary of Recommendations and Prevention Strategies
source_version_date: Current CDC Infection Control pages reviewed/updated 2024; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Summary of Recommendations, section 3 ‘Hand Hygiene and Aseptic Technique,’ recommendations 1, 2, and 6; section 5 ‘Skin Preparation,’ recommendation 2; section 6 ‘Catheter Site Dressing Regimens,’ recommendation 1. Prevention Strategies repeats that clean or sterile gloves may be worn for dressing changes and aseptic technique must be maintained
source_claim_supported: CDC requires hand hygiene and aseptic catheter care, appropriate antiseptic skin preparation during central-line dressing changes, and a sterile catheter-site dressing; either clean or sterile gloves may be used for routine intravascular-catheter dressing changes, whereas maximal sterile barrier precautions apply to central-line insertion rather than routine dressing changes.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control; apply principles of infection prevention, asepsis, and safe management of invasive devices
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic central-venous-catheter dressing care
correction_summary: The source item was clinically overbroad because it stated that a central-line dressing change requires ‘sterile technique throughout.’ Current CDC guidance instead specifies aseptic technique and explicitly allows either clean or sterile gloves for dressing changes while requiring skin antisepsis and a sterile dressing. The item was rebuilt to test this exact distinction and reclassified from Basic Care and Comfort to Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: central venous catheter infection prevention / dressing change
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against current CDC intravascular-catheter recommendations. CDC distinguishes aseptic technique from maximal sterile barrier precautions and explicitly permits either clean or sterile gloves for dressing changes. The original source claim was therefore rejected as too absolute.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A combines only CDC-supported steps: hand hygiene, aseptic technique, antiseptic skin preparation, sterile dressing, and clean-or-sterile gloves. No unsupported glove mandate, timing interval, dressing brand, or universal chlorhexidine concentration beyond the source is introduced into the stem.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct. It accurately integrates the CDC requirements for routine catheter-site dressing care.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect. Prior sterile insertion does not remove the need for aseptic technique during ongoing catheter care.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect. Absence of visible infection does not eliminate recommended skin antisepsis during a dressing change.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect. Maximal sterile barrier precautions are recommended for CVC/PICC insertion or guidewire exchange, not every routine dressing change.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A matches the full CDC dressing-change recommendations. D is deliberately plausible because maximal sterile barriers are correct for insertion, but not for the routine procedure in the stem.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe realistic infection-prevention approaches; the correct answer is not keyed by an obviously safer-sounding but unsupported absolute.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control is the direct NCLEX category because the item tests aseptic care of an invasive vascular device and prevention of catheter-related infection.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited sterile-versus-aseptic terminology, glove requirements, insertion-versus-maintenance barriers, skin antisepsis, sterile dressing requirements, CDC currentness, category mapping, distractor plausibility, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
